feedback: Reward answers that tie survival to change being slower than the generational adaptation rate given available variation.
Challenge answers that say a species 'failed' or 'was weak' — redirect to the rate comparison and specific vulnerability factors.
Prompt for a human-driver when the learner explains current losses only in terms of natural change.
activities.intendedInsight: The argue-from-evidence objective asks learners to turn the rate-race model into a defended explanation of why a given species could not keep pace and why current rates exceed the background rate.
learnerActions: Take part in a role-play interview with a palaeontologist (about the dodo or woolly mammoth) or a conservation biologist (about a species on the brink today).
Respond to the challenge 'Why couldn't it just adapt?' by explaining the rate mismatch and the species' specific vulnerability factors.

Respond to 'Why are today's extinction rates different from normal?' by distinguishing background from mass extinction and naming human drivers (habitat loss, overexploitation, pollution, climate change).
Marshal observations from the survival-race activity into a short, evidence-based argument about whether a named species can keep pace with current change.
activities.title: Argue the case: interview a conservation biologist or palaeontologist

feedback: Full response: explains extinction as change outpacing the generational rate of adaptation given available variation, distinguishes background from mass extinction and endangered from extinct, links current losses to human drivers, and transfers the reasoning to the slow-versus-fast case.

Partial response: recognises that fast change is dangerous but cannot tie it to the mechanism, or cannot distinguish background from mass extinction, or endangered from extinct — reteach by comparing a fast and slow version of the same change.
Gap response endorsing 'animals always evolve quickly enough': tie adaptation to its requirements (pre-existing heritable variation and many generations); evolution is not an on-demand rescue.

If a learner says individuals will remodel their own bodies because they need to: any change within a lifetime is limited and not inherited; adaptation comes from selection acting across generations on heritable variation (mostly already present, with new mutations arising at random), and only if there is time — need does not trigger the right change.

If a learner treats 30 surviving individuals as 'saved': introduce minimum viable population — too few individuals means too little variation, inbreeding and vulnerability to chance events, so a species can be doomed before the last one dies; it is far from safe, even though intensive captive breeding has occasionally rescued species from very low numbers (e.g. California condor).
activities.intendedInsight: A learner who grasps the rate argument rejects 'just evolve in time', ties survival to change being slower than the generational adaptation rate given available variation, separates endangered from extinct (minimum viable population), and separates background from mass extinction.
learnerActions: Judge the claim: 'As the climate warms very fast, don't worry — animals will just evolve quickly to cope, so they won't go extinct.' Decide whether the reasoning is sound and explain when a species CAN adapt in time and when it can't.
Answer the follow-up: the same warming happens slowly over 50,000 years instead of 100 years — does your answer change, and why?
Answer: there are 30 individuals of a species left, all in one zoo — is that species safe? Why or why not?
Explain how the current rate of extinction differs from the background rate and what is driving the difference.
Match each historical case to what outpaced it, and distinguish an example of background extinction from a mass extinction.
